I rushed over, gathered her in my arms, and covered her with tender kisses, pleading:

“Tell me, darling, tell me! What’s wrong?”

Her head dropped weakly against my chest, and she whispered in a breath I could scarcely hear:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I called to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopathic doctor and tell him to come!”

Two minutes later I was kneeling beside our daughter’s crib while Sandy sent servants running in every direction through the palace. I understood almost immediately: membranous croup! I leaned close and whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart. Hello-Central.”

She slowly opened her gentle eyes and managed to say:

“Papa.”

That reassured me. She was still a long way from dying. I ordered sulphur medicines and fetched the kettle used for croup myself. When Sandy or the child falls ill, I don’t sit around waiting for doctors. I knew how to nurse them both and had plenty of practice. Our little one had spent much of her short life in my arms. Often I could ease her distress and make her laugh, with tears still clinging to her eyelashes, when even her mother could not.

Just then Sir Launcelot came striding through the great hall in his finest armour, on his way to the stock exchange. He was its president and sat in the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad. The exchange consisted of the Knights of the Round Table, and these days they used their famous table for business. Seats there cost—well, you would never believe the price, so there is no point giving it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, a trader who generally bet on falling prices. He had cornered the stock of one of the new lines and was preparing that very day to squeeze the short sellers. But what did that matter? He was still the same old Launcelot. Passing the doorway, he glanced inside and learned that his favourite little girl was ill. That settled it. The traders could fight over prices without him; he would come in and do everything possible for little Hello-Central. And he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, fitted a fresh wick to the alcohol lamp, and began heating the croup kettle, all within half a minute. Sandy had meanwhile arranged a blanket canopy over the crib, and we were ready.

Sir Launcelot raised the steam. Together we put unslaked lime and carbolic acid into the kettle, added a little lactic acid, then filled it with water and placed the steam spout beneath the canopy. With everything in order, we sat on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch.

“Unless you choose to call Miss Havisham a he. And I scarcely believe even you would go that length.”

“Miss Havisham, up in town?” Joe asked.

“Is there a Miss Havisham down in town?” my sister retorted.

“She wants this boy sent there to play. Naturally, he is going. And he had better do some playing,” said my sister, shaking her head at me by way of encouraging the utmost gaiety and liveliness, “or I shall make him work.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham up town—as had everyone for miles about—as a lady of immense wealth and grim aspect, who lived secluded in a great gloomy house secured against thieves.

“Well, I never!” said Joe in astonishment. “I wonder how she got acquainted with Pip!”

“Blockhead!” my sister cried. “Who told you she was acquainted with him?”

“Which a certain person,” Joe once more suggested politely, “did mention her wanting him to come and play.”

“Couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew a boy who might come and play? Is it altogether impossible that Uncle Pumblechook should be one of her tenants, and that he should occasionally—we won’t say every quarter or half-year, since that would demand too much of your understanding—but occasionally call to pay the rent? Could she not then inquire whether he knew of a boy to come and play? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, who is perpetually thoughtful and considerate towards us—though you may doubt it, Joseph,” with such profound reproach that one might have supposed him the hardest-hearted nephew alive, “recommend this boy, standing here Prancing”—which I solemnly affirm I was not—“to whom I have always been a willing slave?”

“Excellent again!” Uncle Pumblechook exclaimed. “Well expressed! Finely pointed! Excellent indeed! Now, Joseph, you understand the matter.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister continued reproachfully, while Joe rubbed the back of his hand repeatedly across his nose in apology, “you do not yet understand it, whatever you may think. You may imagine you do, but you do not, Joseph. You don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, perceiving that a visit to Miss Havisham might, for all we can tell, make this boy’s fortune, has offered to drive him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, lodge him overnight, and deliver him himself to Miss Havisham tomorrow morning. And mercy upon me!” she cried, suddenly throwing off her bonnet in desperation, “here I am talking to mere Mooncalfs, with Uncle Pumblechook kept waiting, the mare taking cold outside, and the boy filthy with soot and dirt from the crown of his head to the bottom of his foot!”

He shuddered and stepped back inside, shutting the window after him.

At the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not look at the man he had murdered. The important thing, he felt, was to avoid fully understanding what had happened. The friend who had painted that terrible portrait, the cause of all his suffering, was no longer part of his life. That was all he needed to know.

Then he thought of the lamp. It was an unusual Moorish design, made of dull silver decorated with curling patterns of polished steel and set with rough turquoises. His servant might notice it was missing and ask questions. He paused, then went back and picked it up from the table. This time he could not avoid seeing the dead body. How motionless it was! How dreadful and white the long hands looked! It resembled a horrible figure made of wax.

He locked the door behind him and crept downstairs. The wood creaked, sounding as though it were crying out in pain. Several times he stopped and listened. No—everything was quiet. The noise came only from his own steps.

In the library, he noticed the bag and coat lying in a corner. He would have to hide them. He unlocked a concealed cupboard in the wooden wall panels, where he kept his collection of strange disguises, and put them inside. He could easily burn them later. Then he checked his watch. It was one-forty.

He sat down to think. Every year—almost every month—men in England were hanged for doing what he had done. A murderous madness had been in the air. Some red star had drifted too near the earth.... Yet what proof was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. Nobody had seen him return. Most of the servants were away at Selby Royal. His personal servant had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes, Basil had gone to Paris on the midnight train, exactly as he had planned. He was such a private, reserved man that months would pass before anyone became suspicious. Months! Long before that, everything could be destroyed.

An idea suddenly occurred to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and stepped into the hall. There he stopped. Outside, he heard a policeman’s slow, heavy footsteps on the pavement and saw the beam of the man’s lantern reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

A few moments later he lifted the latch and slipped outside, closing the door very softly behind him. Then he started to ring the bell.
